newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian forces step up fight against militants.
newsitem.headline: Indian forces step up fight against militants.

text.p: Indian security forces have launched an aggressive campaign to track down and kill militants in the mountains of Kashmir, the region's new police chief said.
Gurbachan Jagat, who assumed his post in March, said many Kashmiris were frustrated after seven years of separatist insurgency and more willing to tip off authorities.

"The ground situation has changed. Generally people are fed up with violence and this has led to an increase in information inputs. We are now getting much better information from the people," Jagat told Reuters in a recent interview.
However, very little reliable information has surfaced about four Westerners who were taken hostage in the region two years ago.

Local officials and diplomats said they did not know if the tourists were dead or alive, and many of the militants who may have had information about their fate have been killed in clashes with security forces.

The army, paramilitary forces and police have stepped up cordon-and-search operations in which they encircle an area, often a village or group of villages, force the residents out of their homes and then search the homes and other buildings.

Increasingly the operations are in rural sectors where the militants can move more freely than in cities such as Srinagar, the summer capital of Jammu and Kashmir state, which is dotted by sandbag bunkers draped in camouflaged netting to protect against grenades.
"The militants have gone now to the higher reaches of the mountains and since there is no contact, we have decided to go to the mountains," Jagat said.
He said some 1,200 specially equipped policemen had been trained to live in the mountains.
"We send these boys in groups of 20 to 25 to stay in forests, make contact and eliminate militants. The idea is rather than waiting for them to attack us, we go after them," Jagat said.
He said the security forces had shifted their strategy.

"For the last five, six months we have completely given up being on the defensive," Jagat said. "We are using more manpower for operations, less for static duties now, and with the flow of better information, we are making more contact and more killings."

Pakistan controls one third of the Himalayan region and stakes a claim over the rest. The new police chief said guerrillas continued to cross into Kashmir from Pakistan. Islamabad denies New Delhi's accusations that it trains and arms militants, saying it provides only moral and diplomatic support.
But Jagat accused Pakistan's Inter Service Intelligence (ISI) agency of sending in guerrillas.

"Infiltration attempts are on. There is no let-up as far as ISI and Pakistan are concerned, their efforts are to put more and more men in. This is the period when they can send more people," Jagat said.
More than 30 guerrillas have been killed by Indian soldiers in the last three weeks after crossing into Kashmir from Pakistan, he said.

Jagat denied charges of large-scale human rights violations by security forces. Kashmir's leading separatist coalition, the All Parties Hurriyat (Freedom) Conference (APHC), says there has been a sharp increase in violations by security forces.

"When such large numbers of forces are involved, a couple of cases can take place, and whosoever is found guilty, we punish them. For the APHC, which does not have a mass base, human rights is the good thing to attract people," the police chief said.
"This summer is very important," Jagat said. "So far we have done reasonably well and if we get through it, I think 1998 should be the end of all this."
